{
  "document_classification": {
    "is_summary_style": false,
    "is_full_incident_report": true,
    "contains_multiple_independent_incidents": false,
    "requires_incident_split": false,
    "recommended_output_mode": "single_incident",
    "classification_reason": "The document is a CSB case study centered on one primary incident at the EQ hazardous waste facility in Apex, North Carolina on October 5, 2006. It contains a dedicated incident description, chronology of response and evacuation, background, analysis, regulatory analysis, conclusions, and recommendations. Although other incidents are mentioned in analysis for comparison, they are not independently developed as separate incident narratives within this document."
  },
  "incidents": [
    {
      "incident_id": "incident_1",
      "is_independent_incident": true,
      "time_reference": "October 5, 2006",
      "incident_summary_section": {
        "section_title": "Introduction",
        "text": "Introduction 
This case study examines a fire 
at a hazardous waste facility 
located in Apex, North Carolina. 
City officials ordered thousands 
of local residents to evacuate for 
two days. About 30 people 
sought medical attention. The 
CSB makes recommendations to 
the US Environmental Protection 
Agency and Environmental 
Technology Council to address 
emergency planning and fire 
protection requirements for 
hazardous waste facilities."
      },
      "incident_description_section": {
        "section_title": "1.0 Incident Description",
        "text": "1.0 Incident Description 
This case study examines a fire at the 
Environmental Quality Company (EQ) 
hazardous waste facility in Apex, North 
Carolina, and the subsequent community 
evacuation. 
At 9:38 pm on October 5, 2006, a citizen 
driving past the EQ facility called 911 to 
report a haze with a “strong chlorine smell.” 
The Apex 911 center dispatched emergency 
personnel to investigate. 
Responding Apex Fire Department 
personnel discovered a chemical cloud 
coming from one of several businesses on 
Investment Boulevard. The Apex Fire 
Chief, acting as the Incident Commander 
(IC), sent two firefighter reconnaissance 
teams in personal protective equipment to 
investigate the source of the cloud. 
Firefighters located a small “sofa-size” fire 
in one of the hazardous waste bays at the EQ 
facility. Within minutes, the fire spread to 
the flammable liquid storage area, causing 
55-gallon drums of flammable hazardous 
waste to explode and sending fireballs 
hundreds of feet into the air. The hazardous 
waste building ultimately collapsed (cover 
photograph). 
During the incident, about 30 people 
(including 13 first responders) sought 
medical attention at local hospitals for 
respiratory distress and nausea. Some were 
treated; none was admitted. 
1.1 Emergency Response 
Because of the unknown nature of the 
burning chemicals and the exploding drums, 
the IC chose to take only defensive actions 
to 
• minimize the risk to emergency 
personnel and community residents, and 
• allow the fire to burn and consume the 
chemicals within the facility. 
The defensive actions included 
• ordering a precautionary evacuation of 
thousands of residents in the surrounding 
community,1
 
• controlling access on roads leading into 
the evacuation area, 
• stopping rail traffic through the 
community, and 
• closing the air space over the facility. 
EQ contracted an industrial firefighting and 
environmental cleanup company with 
specialized equipment to extinguish the fire 
and clean up the site. The contractor 
• built sand berms to minimize water 
runoff that could possibly contaminate 
an adjacent stream, 
• removed the roof and structural steel to 
access the burning waste, 
• extinguished the fire with foam, and 
• removed all debris and hazardous waste 
from the site. 
1.2 Community Evacuation 
The evacuation area included about 3,300 
residences, the town hall, a fire station, and 
the town 911 center.2
 Officials established 
an Emergency Operations Center (EOC) 
outside of the evacuation area to provide a 
safe gathering place for emergency 
responders, state and federal officials, and 
media representatives. 
Evacuees from the community sheltered at 
designated elementary schools, in hotels, or 
with relatives outside the evacuation area. 
The Red Cross, other community 
organizations, and businesses assisted 
residents by providing bedding, food, and 
communication services. 
The IC continued the evacuation order for 
two days because of potential re-ignition and 
persistent smoke from the smoldering 
rubble. 
1.3 Environmental Impact 
The North Carolina Department of 
Environmental and Natural Resources 
(NCDENR) Divisions of Air Quality, Water 
Quality, Environmental Heath, and Waste 
Management and the US Environmental 
Protection Agency (EPA) responded to the 
incident. In the early morning of October 6, 
2006, (about five hours after the fire was 
first reported) the NCDENR and the EPA 
began air monitoring within the evacuation 
area. In addition to ground level 
monitoring, the EPA conducted 10 fly-overs 
with its Airborne Spectral Photographic 
Environmental Collection Technology 
(ASPECT) aircraft. 
EQ also contracted with a company 
specializing in environmental monitoring, 
testing and assessment to conduct ground 
level atmospheric monitoring beginning 
October 6, 2006. 
In the weeks following the incident, the 
NCDENR looked for residual contamination 
by conducting soil, indoor environmental, 
and exterior swipe sampling for a range 
organic and inorganic materials.3
 On 
November 17, 2006, the NCDENR reported 
that “environmental tests show no offsite 
contamination from EQ fire.”"
      },
      "other_related_sections": [
        {
          "section_title": "3.2 Fire Detection",
          "text": "3.2 Fire Detection 
Even though the facility stored hundreds of 
55-gallon drums of flammable and 
combustible materials, the EQNC hazardous 
waste building was not required to be 
equipped with fire or smoke detection 
sensors nor monitored after hours (nights or 
weekends). 
Continuous monitoring by personnel or with 
remotely monitored sensors can alert 
company personnel and first responders at 
the inception of a fire. This may provide 
first responders additional time to initiate 
emergency actions before the situation 
grows out of control."
        },
        {
          "section_title": "3.3 Fire Control Equipment",
          "text": "3.3 Fire Control Equipment 
Portable fire extinguishers were the only fire 
control equipment in the EQNC hazardous 
waste building. The facility included 
segregated areas (storage bays) for different 
waste types separated by six-inch-high 
curbs. The curbs could contain spills within 
the bays, but would not prevent a fire from 
spreading from one bay to another. 
The initial “sofa-size” fire observed by 
firefighters was in the oxidizer bay where a 
fiberboard container of unspent aircraft 
oxygen generators10 and containers of solid 
chlorine-based pool chemicals were 
awaiting final shipment.11 Figure 2 shows 
an oxygen generator found in the debris with 
its activation pin in place, indicating that it 
was unspent when the fire started. Because 
oxygen generators were located at or near 
the origin of the fire and, when exposed to 
fire, produce oxygen that significantly 
increases the intensity of a fire, the CSB 
concluded that the unspent oxygen 
generators most likely contributed to the 
rapid spread of the fire to the adjacent bay 
where flammable hazardous wastes were 
stored. 
While not required, had EQNC used fire 
barriers (walls) to separate the segregated 
waste bays, the fire would likely have been 
contained within the oxidizer bay, 
significantly mitigating the incident’s 
consequences. 
The National Fire Protection Association 
(NFPA) publishes fire protection standards 
for many industrial facility types12 (e.g. 
NFPA 820, “Standard for Fire Protection in 
Wastewater Treatment and Collection 
Facilities”). These standards address fire 
protection requirements specific to the 
facility type. However, no standard 
specifically addresses fire protection for 
hazardous waste treatment, storage, and 
disposal facilities. 
A review by CSB of fire protection practices 
in use at 12 other hazardous waste 
facilities13 showed wide variation. Some 
facilities use active fire suppression systems 
to control or extinguish fires, some use fire 
barriers, and others, like EQNC, rely only on 
portable fire extinguishers."
        },
        {
          "section_title": "3.4 Emergency Planning",
          "text": "3.4 Emergency Planning 
Apex fire personnel identified the EQNC 
facility as the source of the chemical cloud 
and fire; however, EQNC had not provided 
any detailed written information on the 
types, quantities, and location of hazardous 
materials in the facility to fire personnel or 
the Local Emergency Planning Committee 
(LEPC). Additionally, since the EQNC 
facility was unoccupied at the time of the 
incident, no emergency coordinator was on-
site to initiate the facility contingency plan14 
or assess the extent of the release or 
emergency. 
Other companies in the Town of Apex 
provided information to the fire department 
on the types, quantities, and location of 
hazardous materials the companies handled. 
The fire department used this information 
for emergency planning and conducted joint 
emergency drills with several of these 
companies. 
When companies provide written 
information on the approximate quantity, 
hazards, and location of materials within 
their facilities to fire departments, police 
departments, hospitals, and LEPCs, 
responders can preplan for emergencies."
        }
      ],
      "extraction_notes": "Single primary incident extracted. The Introduction was used as the incident summary section. The full 1.0 Incident Description section was extracted through the next top-level header (2.0 Background), including subsections 1.1 through 1.3 because they describe consequence development, emergency response, evacuation, and environmental impact. Additional hazard-evolution and consequence-related analysis sections 3.2, 3.3, and 3.4 were included. Comparative incident references in section 3.1 were not treated as separate incidents because they are brief contextual examples rather than full incident narratives in this document."
    }
  ]
}

accident_scenario_schema_definition:
SCHEMA DEFINITION

The output must strictly follow the provided JSON schema. Each field has a specific meaning and must be filled according to the rules below.

General Rules

Evidence

The "evidence" field must contain a short quote copied directly from the source that supports the extracted value.

If source = "incident_description":
The evidence must be copied verbatim from the incident report text.

Do not invent, paraphrase, or infer evidence.

If no supporting evidence can be found, set:
evidence = "N/A"
source = "Not specified".

Source

The "source" field indicates where the information was obtained, the allowed source are listed in each nodes.

Allowed values:

incident_description  
Information directly extracted from the incident report.


Not specified  
Used when the information cannot be determined from the incident report or reliable external knowledge sources.

Node ID

Each node must include a `node_id`, which serves as a unique identifier in the graph.

The `node_id` must follow the prefix corresponding to the node type:

- H#  → HazardConsequence nodes
- En# → Entity nodes
- C#  → Condition nodes
- Ev# → Event nodes

Where # is a sequential integer starting from 1 within each node category.

Examples:
H1, En1, C1, Ev1

Rules:
- Each node must have exactly one `node_id`.
- All `node_id` values must be unique within the output.
- The prefix must match the node's `node_type`.
- Do not invent other ID formats.
- The `node_id` is only an identifier and must not contain semantic meaning.

--------------------------------------------------
Material
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The hazardous substance involved in the accident scenario.

This refers to the chemical or material present in the process that participates in the release, dispersion, ignition, or hazard consequence.


--------------------------------------------------
Location
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The physical place or equipment where the accident-related event occurs.

This may include process units, storage tanks, pipelines, packaging areas, or other facility locations relevant to the accident.


--------------------------------------------------
Phase
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The physical phase of the material at the time of the accident.

This condition describes whether the material exists as liquid, vapor, solid, or a two-phase mixture, which can influence release behavior and hazard consequences.


--------------------------------------------------
Temperature
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The temperature condition of the material or environment during the accident scenario.

Temperature can affect vapor generation, chemical stability, and the likelihood of ignition or hazardous reactions.

--------------------------------------------------
Pressure
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The pressure condition of the material or process system during the accident scenario.

Pressure influences the containment, release rate, and phase behavior of the material.
Elevated pressure can increase the driving force for a release and accelerate discharge from equipment, while low or atmospheric pressure conditions may affect vapor formation and dispersion behavior.

--------------------------------------------------
Volatility
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The tendency of a substance to vaporize.

High volatility substances can easily form flammable or toxic vapor clouds that may contribute to explosion or dispersion hazards.


--------------------------------------------------
Combustibility
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the material is capable of burning in the presence of an ignition source.

Combustible materials can participate in fires or explosions when mixed with air and exposed to ignition.


--------------------------------------------------
ToxicSubstance
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the material has toxic properties that can cause harm to humans or the environment.

Toxic substances may produce hazardous exposure through vapor dispersion or direct contact.


--------------------------------------------------
Asphyxiant
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the substance can cause oxygen displacement or interfere with oxygen transport in the body.

Asphyxiants may lead to suffocation or oxygen deficiency hazards in confined or poorly ventilated spaces.


--------------------------------------------------
Conductivity
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The electrical conductivity property of the material.

Low conductivity liquids may accumulate static electricity during transfer operations, increasing the risk of static discharge ignition.


--------------------------------------------------
ReleaseType
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The manner in which hazardous material is released into the environment.

This condition distinguishes between instantaneous releases and continuous releases, which influence dispersion behavior and accident escalation.


--------------------------------------------------
IgnitionSource
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The source of energy that can ignite a flammable mixture.

Examples include static electricity sparks, open flames, hot surfaces, electrical equipment, or mechanical sparks.


--------------------------------------------------
Confinement
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The degree to which flammable or hazardous material is enclosed within a confined space.

High confinement can increase explosion overpressure and significantly influence explosion severity.


--------------------------------------------------
Dispersion
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The spreading of released material into the surrounding environment.

Dispersion determines how vapors, gases, or toxic substances distribute in air and whether hazardous concentrations can form.


--------------------------------------------------
MechanicalFailure
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
A physical failure of equipment that contributes to the accident.

This may include rupture, leakage, seal failure, structural failure, or malfunction of process equipment that leads to loss of containment.

If a mechanical failure clearly occurred and contributed to the accident,
but the exact failed component or exact failure mode cannot be determined
from the incident description, use "Unknown mechanical failure" as the name.

Use "Not specified" only when the incident description does not provide enough
support to identify whether a mechanical failure should be represented at all.

--------------------------------------------------
InitiatingEvent
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The first abnormal operational or physical event
that directly initiates the accident sequence
within the process system.

The initiating event may summarize closely related
operational actions and conditions that immediately
lead to the hazardous sequence.

--------------------------------------------------
IgnitionSource Special Rule
--------------------------------------------------

If ignition clearly occurred in the incident, but the exact ignition source
cannot be determined from the incident description, use
"Unknown ignition source" as the name.

Use "Not specified" only when the incident description does not provide enough
support to identify whether an ignition source should be represented at all.
